# Related Literature {#sec-literature}

<!-- STUB. Sources: Paper/sections/30-related_lit.qmd (skeleton), 30-lit-rev.qmd (notes) -->

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

**Positioning summary (draft only, 2026-09-24).** The validation-sample idea is old (traces of income). The novelty is using the production function to account for firms' heterogeneity in productivity (size) and juridical organization, with corporations as the truth-reporting sample. The method needs only reported inputs and output, so it works on standard firm surveys and equally on administrative records. Public economics is the primary audience; production functions are secondary; the econometrics of unobservables is a toolbox, not a contribution, and belongs in a related-literature section (thesis only).

| Role | Strand | Key references | Their approach and limitation | What this paper does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary | Measuring firm evasion | @Carrillo2022, @Carrillo2017, @Asatryan2017, @Zumaya2021, @Pomeranz2015 (tax records); @Dabla2019 (survey) | Tax-record studies need confidential administrative data, available for few countries. Survey studies rely on self-reported shares of sales declared (World Bank Enterprise Surveys), with productivity proxied by sales per worker. | Identifies overreporting from reported inputs and output only, so it applies to standard firm surveys and to administrative records alike. |
| Primary | Validation samples (traces of income) | @Pissarides1989, @Paulus2015, @Gorodnichenko2009 | An indirect measure of true income (consumption) compared between a group that cannot misreport (employees, whose income is third-party reported) and the self-employed. @Gorodnichenko2009 use the consumption–income gap to estimate how evasion responded to Russia's 2001 flat-tax reform. Built for individuals, and assumes both groups share the same consumption–income relation. | Same validation logic, applied to firms: corporations are the truth-reporting sample, and the production function accounts for heterogeneity in productivity (size) and juridical organization. |
| Primary | Tax rates and evasion | @Slemrod2019, @FismanWei2004, @HandleyMoore2017, @Yitzhaki1974 | The sign of the effect of the rate is ambiguous in theory. Evidence on rates is scarce, because governments randomize enforcement, not rates; what exists comes mostly from misreported imports. Enforcement studies show firms adjust reported costs (@Carrillo2017, @Asatryan2017). | Evidence from a statutory rate change (the 1983 reform, @sec-fiscal), and a structural counterfactual over the tax rate (@sec-counterfactual). |
| Primary | Tax rates, revenue and optimal taxation with evasion | @Feldstein1999, @SlemrodKopczuk2002, @Chetty2009, @Saez2012; @Cremer1993, @KeenSlemrod2017; @Best2015 | The revenue response to rates is measured through the elasticity of taxable income, which bundles evasion, avoidance and real responses, for individuals. Theory lowers optimal rates on goods where evasion responds more to the rate (@Cremer1993) and treats enforcement through its own revenue elasticity (@KeenSlemrod2017). Firm-level evidence comes from bunching at kinks and notches: taxing turnover rather than profits can raise revenue by cutting evasion (@Best2015). | A structural, firm-level estimate of how input overreporting responds to the purchases-side rate, and a counterfactual for deduction claims over the rate (@sec-counterfactual). |
| Secondary | Production functions and productivity | @Gandhi2020, @Ackerberg2015, @Levinsohn2003; @Collard2020 | Proxy-variable methods assume reported inputs are true. Work on misreported inputs treats it as mean-zero measurement error, mostly in capital. | Treats overreporting as an optimal choice (not mean zero, possibly correlated with productivity) in the flexible input that identification relies on; corrects elasticities and productivity (@sec-pf). |
| Related literature only (thesis) | Econometrics of unobservables | @Hu2008, @Hu2022, @Schennach2021, @Schennach2014 | Identification and estimation with latent variables. | Methods applied, no contribution claimed: deconvolution (@sec-deconvolution) and ELVIS (@sec-counterfactual). |

:::
